synthesis.description: The real-time desk confirms and corrects each day's power schedules. The desk lead tells traders where the desk is long or short by zone and hour and asks them to buy or sell to fill, booking deals to the right book in Enpower. Preschedulers pass EPE schedule sheets and lending arrangements, which real time checks against Enpower and CAISO or CAPS records; wrong import IDs, volumes, duplicates and prices are flagged and fixed. Cuts and derates mean calling counterparties at the top of the hour, entering cuts in Enpower path confirmation, re-tagging, and zeroing and valuing cut deals.

Real time checks the schedule sheet against Enpower deals and CAISO or CAPS records by hour.
Shorts and longs are filled by buying or selling at the stated points and booked to the right book.
Wrong import IDs, volumes, duplicates or deal prices are flagged and corrected with preschedulers.
Cuts and derates are handled: counterparties called, cuts entered in path confirmation, tags updated.
Cut deals are zeroed out and valued, and revenue is routed to volume management.
The desk lead circulates follow-up rules and corrections to the shift.

stalls.summary: CAISO systems fail the desk: its computers went down and hours had to be submitted ahead of the outage, and on another day it again had difficulties reading the desk's bids.
The EPE schedule sheet keeps arriving incomplete or wrong, day after day: duplicate schedules, wrong lending volumes and wrong hourly figures that real time has to square away with the preschedulers.

Deals need correcting after entry: a deal price is changed in Enpower and revenue then shows in the wrong place, CAPS shows a final import different from the desk's records, and email to Real Time is reminded to match what is entered in Enpower.
Records for a period were lost, so those on shift had to work out which deals were done and reconstruct the sheet.
A reference manual for handling cuts is asked for, but the reply is that there is no time today and it may wait till tomorrow; cut procedures are circulated separately later.

contradictions.summary: Who prepares the EPE schedules is unsettled within one exchange: the preschedule lead says she and the desk lead are considering having Real Time take over the EPE preschedules, while the same thread names Diane Cutsforth as the one working on the EPE schedule.

Prices on El Paso Electric lending and purchase deals conflict: a lending schedule is announced at a low price, a related deal is later re-priced much higher in Enpower with the resulting revenue disputed, and another round has EPE purchases reduced back to the low price.

Schedule records disagree with what was arranged: lending from PSCO in the EPE schedules shows a different volume from the agreed one, SPS is wrong for an hour, an import ID carries the wrong on-peak and off-peak volumes, and CAPS shows a firm import the desk did not expect.

automation.approach: A checkout report that lines up the prescheduling sheet, Enpower deals and CAISO or CAPS final schedules hour by hour and flags mismatched volumes, wrong import IDs, duplicates, missing interchange deals, untagged schedules and prices that differ from the agreed figure. Pair it with a shift checklist covering hourly counterparty calls, cut entry in path confirmation, tagging both load periods, and zeroing and valuing cut deals.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same checks repeated by hand and the same errors found late. A shift checklist gives traders the cut and tagging rules that now arrive as scattered emails, and the cross-check can catch sheet errors before real time inherits them; buying, calling counterparties and judging cuts stay with traders.

synthesis.description: Logistics and volume management staff find gas that flowed at a meter with no deal, an expired deal ticket, no nomination or no transport contract. They check the ticket in Sitara and email the trader or desk with the meter, period and volumes, asking for a deal to be created or extended, which transport contract to use, or what price to bill. The trader enters the ticket and replies with the deal number, and the volumes are reallocated. Old uncovered flow sits under the HPL Strangers Gas account or goes for approval to write off to Unaccounted for Gas.
steps: Logistics or volume staff spot flow at a meter for a period with no valid deal, an expired ticket or no nomination.
They check the deal ticket and contract in Sitara to confirm the gap and its dates.
They email the trader or desk with meter, period and volumes, asking for a deal, an extension, a contract or a price.
The trader settles price and terms, creates or extends the deal ticket in Sitara and replies with the deal number.
Volumes are reallocated to the new or extended deal and its transport contract.
Long-uncovered volumes are booked to a holding account or sent for write-off approval.
Unanswered requests are chased or forwarded to someone else.

stalls.summary: Requests wait on answers from traders and schedulers: senders note they never heard back on which transport contract to use, ask for status on open meters, and wait for a person to return before the deal can be done.

It is often unclear who should act: requesters ask colleagues to sort out between themselves who rolls the deal, forward the request to another person, apologise for leaving someone off the thread, or are told to talk to someone else.
Work is redone when the first answer is wrong: a deal number offered was not a deal between ENA and HPL, and a spot ticket request had its price corrected after it was sent.
Systems get in the way: a deal errors out against its gathering contract, and flow cannot yet carry over to the downstream system after a ticket is entered.
Uncovered flow is left for long periods: logistics raises flow from long-past production months, volumes sit under the strangers gas account, and a deal is requested well after the month it covers.
The same gap recurs because deal tickets and their contracts expire while gas keeps flowing at the meter, so each lapse starts a new round.

contradictions.summary: Different people are named as the one who handles erroring or missing deals: one message says Daren used to handle it, and the same sender then says Danny Conner handles it, while an outside party points to Daren Farmer to put the deal in.

Uncovered volumes are treated in different ways across rounds: booked under the strangers gas account, written off to unaccounted-for gas, or given a new deal, and one sender asks outright whether it should be a buyback, force majeure or no deal.

One message says Volume Management must set up the accounting arrangements to cover the volume, while another sender takes responsibility for the interconnect ticket not being adjusted, leaving it unclear which side owns the fix.

automation.approach: An exception report matches measured flow by meter and day against active deal tickets, nominations and transport contracts in Sitara, flags flow with no deal and tickets about to expire while the meter still flows, and routes each item to the meter's assigned owner with the period and volumes filled in. A written procedure sets who creates or extends deals by desk, the fields a request must carry, and how long-uncovered volumes are treated.
automation.rationale: Most stalls are waiting on the right person and confusion over who acts, and the contradictions are over ownership and over how uncovered volumes are booked. A procedure that names the owner, the required request fields and the treatment of old volumes addresses those directly; the exception report then removes the manual hunt for gaps.

estimated.rationale: Each round means pulling scheduled, actualized and meter volumes for the points or deals in question, finding the cause of the variance and correcting tickets, allocations or imbalance records; some rounds also compile point lists, update month-to-date flow sheets or make manual entries to clear past balances. A single meter or deal check takes about 20 minutes, a typical round 45, a multi-party list or write-off up to 150. A variance report could take over lookups and matching; diagnosis, counterparty agreement and approvals stay manual.

synthesis.description: A round starts when someone notices that scheduled, confirmed, actualized or measured gas volumes disagree at a meter, on a deal or in a pipeline imbalance statement. Settlements, volume management, measurement or the counterparty asks logistics to verify the nomination, path or allocation; the scheduler checks deals and meter data, moves volumes or updates tickets, and imbalance statements or month-to-date flow numbers are resent. They email logistics or volume management asking for the nomination, path, allocation or deal to be verified.
The scheduler checks nominations, deal tickets and meter data and explains or finds the cause of the variance.
Volumes are moved or re-allocated, deals and storage or injection tickets are updated or created.
Updated imbalance figures or month-to-date flow numbers are sent to the customer, pipeline or internal group.
Old or prior-period balances are cleared by payback, manual book entries or an approved write-off to unaccounted-for gas.

stalls.summary: Requesters wait on answers: earlier voice mails and requests go unanswered, issues get no updates, internal customers ask when results will be ready, and prior-month data has to be retrieved before work can continue.

Handoffs are unclear: people do not know which group a request comes from, misunderstand what was wanted when work was handed over, and ask who needs to talk to whom to fix volumes that were never actualized.
A requester needing an urgent answer is told the fix is not a priority item, so the round stalls until someone escalates.
Issues go round and round between groups without being resolved.
The scheduling system cannot process a payback for a past period, so the imbalance has to be cleared with manual entries outside it.
Old balances are left alone: nobody wants to touch them so they sit with one person, old customer balances are cleared long after the fact, and write-offs wait for approval.

contradictions.summary: Ownership of the daily imbalance check is disputed: Mary Poorman says it has been Bill's since the reorg, Bill Williams says Darron has owned it since March, and Mary Poorman also says the unwanted work just sits with her.
In the same round one party was told the measurement problem was not a priority item while another demanded an answer as soon as possible.
Measurement replies to set the record straight that it was neither contacted nor informed, disputing the account of the issue given earlier in the thread.

automation.approach: A scheduled comparison of scheduled, nominated, actualized and metered volumes by meter, deal and counterparty could flag variances above a tolerance, list open imbalances with their named owner and age, and generate the imbalance statement or month-to-date flow summary for the counterparty. A written procedure would name the owner of the daily imbalance check, the contacts in measurement, volume management and settlements, and the route for manual entries and write-off approval.
automation.rationale: The stalls are mostly about who owns the check, who to ask and how to clear old balances the system cannot handle, and the mail disputes ownership outright. A procedure naming owners, contacts and the clearing and write-off route addresses those first; the variance report then removes the repetitive lookups and matching once the routing is settled.

Matching statement lines to deals could be automated; resolving the dispute stays manual.

synthesis.description: Settlement and volume analysts check invoices, payments, demand charges and ISO settlement charges or revenues against the deals booked in Sitara, and resolve differences with counterparties and traders. The analyst researches deal tickets and prices, asks the trader or scheduler to verify or correct Sitara, and settles with the counterparty; some disputes need trader tapes pulled.

The analyst looks up the deal ticket, volumes and pricing in Sitara for the days in question.
The analyst asks the trader, scheduler or deal owner to verify the price or explain the deal.
Sitara deals or prices are corrected, or deals are separated or netted as agreed.
The difference is resolved with the counterparty by call or corrected invoice, with recordings pulled when a trade itself is disputed.
ISO charges and revenues are allocated to the right trading group and disputes are raised with the ISO.

Analysts do not know who handles a deal, invoice or counterparty, or that the usual contact is out, so items are forwarded around before anyone works them.
Deal records are missing or out of date: Sitara was not updated for a month, and no Sitara deal can be found for an invoiced amount.
Outside systems fail the review: awarded ISO prices did not match the bids, and settlement information from the Hub arrives late.
Some disputes stay open across several messages, such as an ISO amount still unresolved after earlier mail about it.

contradictions.summary: Company and counterparty prices disagree: the company paid one price while the counterparty says its price was higher, and other rounds report price differences and price issues with suppliers for past production months.

Settlement figures conflict with the company's own expectations: published ISO prices did not match bids, a capacity payment is said to be lower than it should be, and a charge for a reduced purchase is disputed.
Deal records disagree between the parties: the company invoiced a deal the counterparty cannot find in its system, and a counterparty does not know why it received a payment.

Responsibility for deals and meters is stated differently from message to message: one deal is said to be handled going forward by one analyst, another sender only knows by hearsay who handles a deal, and meters are reassigned to one person while another is named as allocating a point.

automation.approach: A reconciliation report that matches counterparty invoices, payments and ISO settlement lines to Sitara deals by deal number, day, volume and price and lists only the variances, with each variance entered in a shared dispute log that records the counterparty, the named owner, the trader asked to verify, and the status.
automation.rationale: Most rounds start with someone hunting for a deal or price and then waiting on whoever owns it. A variance report removes the hunt, and a log with named owners and status cuts the chasing and forwarding, while settling each dispute with the counterparty stays a judgment call.

synthesis.description: Customers, suppliers and plants such as the Enron Methanol plant and Calpine send daily or monthly gas nominations, usually as attached documents or spreadsheets. Schedulers forward them to whoever schedules the affected pipeline or meters, estimate volumes where none arrive (from the prior year's nomination or a recent average), enter volumes against deals and pipeline paths, confirm deal numbers, meters and transport numbers, and issue revised nominations when flows, meters or spot purchases change.
steps: A customer, supplier or plant sends a daily or monthly nomination, usually as an attached document or spreadsheet.
The scheduler forwards it to the people who schedule the affected pipeline, trade zone or meters.
Where no nomination arrives, the scheduler estimates volumes from the prior year's nomination or a recent average.
Volumes are entered against deals and pipeline paths in the scheduling system.
Deal numbers, meters and transport numbers are confirmed with the counterparty or internal desks.
When flows, meters or purchases change, a revised nomination is issued and the path or volume corrected.
At month end, schedulers pull their own meters from the position and confirm them back to the lead scheduler.

stalls.summary: Rounds wait on replies: a check goes unanswered, a producer does not respond after repeated voice and email contacts, a transport number is still outstanding, and a meter addition waits on a return call.
Nominations are reworked after the fact: a mistake in the start-of-month nominations, a pipeline path changed by another scheduler, and revised daily nominations reissued by the customer.
The month position attachment keeps bouncing off the mail gateway, so it is pasted into the message body instead.
Confirmation is held up until deal numbers are supplied, and some nominations are left pending while a colleague decides whether to wait on them.
Who places which nominations shifts: a suggestion to centralize transport nominations, and a later assignment of off-system nominations to one scheduler.

automation.approach: A standard nomination form (day, meter, pipeline, deal and volume) that customers and suppliers fill in, loaded into the scheduling system by a script that compares each nomination with the prior one and with flowing volumes, flags missing deal or transport numbers and disconnected meters, and drafts the revised nomination for a scheduler to review when volumes change.
automation.rationale: Nominations arrive in varied formats (documents, spreadsheets, pasted text) and volumes are re-keyed, estimated and corrected by hand. One shared form removes the re-keying and makes errors such as a wrong start-of-month nomination or a changed path visible before they reach the pipeline, while schedulers keep the judgement on estimates and exceptions.

Pulling standard documents is mechanical; explanations and research on disputed deals are not.

The risk coordinator forwards it to the desk contact who holds the data, such as Pat Ryder for West desk requests.
Desk or risk staff pull deal tickets, confirmations, P&L top sheets or MTM valuations from their systems.
Staff write explanations where asked: where origination value comes from, which index was used, how a difference was booked.
The coordinator collects replies, re-requests anything missing or misplaced, and passes the package to the auditors.
All requests are logged in a matrix circulated for the quarter.

Requests are passed along until they reach whoever can research the deals, such as the real time coordinator for hourly deals.

automation.rationale: The repeated cost is routing: one coordinator forwards every request and presses the desks, and different people are named for West desk requests. A written procedure naming the owner and source for each request type removes that guesswork. Document pulls are mechanical and suit a report; explanations to the auditors need people.

Lists run from a single deal to several counterparties' deals, so 10 to 90 minutes with about 30 in the middle. synthesis.description: Staff on the gas and power desks report faults in trading, scheduling and position tools (Sitara, POPS, MIPS, Unify, Enpower, Position Manager, FSP, Tagg, the El Paso scrape) to application or IT contacts, and the reports are often forwarded around the desk. Support diagnoses the cause and replies with a fix or workaround, such as mapping a drive or pointing a bridge program at another source.
For enhancements, a coordinator compiles the requested changes by business unit and circulates the list for comment.
Before a release or after maintenance, desks name designated testers, who enter test deals, import schedules or exercise the new feature.
Testers report results back, and outage notices are passed to the desk so work is planned around the downtime.

stalls.summary: Tools fail in day-to-day use: actualization problems in MIPS, errors launching a program or logging on to a server, and a new version missing curve data, each stopping the work until support responds.

Position and volume data come out wrong and have to be reconciled by hand: excessive flow showing in POPS, a short position in Position Manager that is still not working properly weeks later, and TDS position problems.

Planned outages and scrape failures leave systems unavailable for stretches, including weekend maintenance on Enpower, CAPS and the POPS server, Sitara downtime, and an El Paso scrape down through a night shift.
Some failures are local setup problems, such as an unmapped H drive or a missing browser when importing finals, that recur machine by machine until each is fixed.
Follow-through on reported problems is weak: a manager complains of a lack of accountability and no sense of urgency, and a long-demonstrated replacement position manager is still being asked after.

automation.approach: A single issue form or log capturing the system, the exact error text, the affected deals or positions and the desk, with status visible to the requester; a standard post-maintenance and release test checklist (log on, enter and check test deals, import schedules, compare positions); a shared outage calendar fed from IT notices; and a short self-help list of known local fixes such as drive mapping.
automation.rationale: Much of the hands-on work is testing after releases and maintenance and triaging repeat faults. A checklist gives designated testers the same steps each time and lets support clear known local problems quickly, while diagnosing new faults and deciding which enhancements to build stays with people.

After a weekend the on-call person sends notes of calls from gas control and producers, cuts and nomination changes, and the desk checks the meters named.
steps: A manager collects vacation requests and sets the weekend or holiday on-call schedule for the desk.
Before an absence the desk member names who covers each desk, meter or pipeline and a point person with a contact number.
The schedule and coverage notice go to the desk, with changes emailed and written on the schedule.
Extra coverage or shift notices, such as dispatch for another office or system downtime, are sent ahead of the shift.

After the shift the on-call notes are written up and sent to the desk.
Desk members check the meters named in the notes and carry weekend changes into regular scheduling.

automation.rationale: The mail shows coverage notices retyped for every absence, schedules changed without being recorded, and free-text weekend notes that the desk then has to turn into meter checks. A notes form and roster layout can be used at once and make hand-backs after the shift easier to act on; deciding who covers stays with the managers.

estimated.rationale: Hands-on work is placing the order by phone or with deployments, gathering turret IDs and desk details, arranging cable and installation, checking receipt against an invoice, and setting up or cancelling phone plans and working out usage. synthesis.description: A round starts with a role change, a reorganisation or a new point or account. A manager such as the logistics lead announces who will handle which pooling points, industrial accounts, pipelines, counterparties or books; the people giving up and taking over the work confirm the transition, pass on how the accounts are run and point others to the new contact. Gaps surface when someone finds an operational account left unassigned or asks who covers it for the new month, and staff moving roles are asked to pick up rates or tasks from others.
steps: A role change, reorganisation or new point or account triggers a reassignment.
A manager decides who takes which pipelines, points, accounts or books.
The changes are announced to logistics and the affected groups.
The outgoing person transitions the accounts and explains the work to the new owner.
The new owner confirms the takeover and is named as the contact for others.
Items later found unassigned are raised and given an owner.

stalls.summary: Work is left without an owner after a reassignment: an operational account is noticed as unassigned and a later question about who covers it for the new month stays unresolved.

People handed new work do not know how to do it: a person asked to pick up off-system pipeline rates has no idea where to start, and an outgoing scheduler says the new owner would not have known how to handle one account.

contradictions.summary: The industrial accounts handover is described inconsistently: Kenneth Seaman says they should be completely transitioned to Robert and Robert Lloyd announces he has taken over all of them, while Kenneth Seaman's reply disputes how the Valero work would have been handled before he leaves Robert to the accounts.

automation.approach: One shared responsibility roster listing each point, account, pipeline and book with its primary owner, backup and effective date, updated by every announcement, with a check before each month starts that lists anything without an owner. Each transfer would come with a short handover list of the accounts' quirks for the new owner.
automation.rationale: The stalls are items left unassigned and new owners unsure of the work, and the announcements are free-text lists that are hard to check. A roster layout gives one place to see who owns what and spot gaps; the handover notes travel with it. Deciding assignments and training stay with people.

steps: A customer emails a request for a price on a stated gas volume and delivery point, or for a hedge, swap or fixed forward purchase.
The recipient forwards the request to the colleague who handles pricing, or asks a colleague to call the customer.
That person checks with the traders for a quote or bid.
The quote is given back to the customer by phone or email.

automation.approach: A standard quote-request message or form that captures product, volume, delivery point, term and the date a reply is needed, routed straight to the trading desk contact, with an indicative price pulled from the current curve for the trader to confirm before calling the customer.
automation.rationale: Requests arrive with the logistics contact and get forwarded around before a trader sees them, and the recipient has to go back to the traders for the terms. A template that carries every term in one message gets the request to the right person complete; setting the price and talking to the customer stay with people.

Send the draft to the connecting pipeline or producer.
Handle counterparty conditions, such as changing the name on the contract before execution.

steps: Record the origination recognized overnight and the desk it came from.
Tell the counterpart book how much was recognized.
Compare the counterpart's recognized amount with what appears in the own book.
Trace any origination an originator reports as missing.
Book corrections to the right cost centre and period to fix the quarter's P&L.

automation.rationale: The recurring work is comparing recognized amounts across books and chasing items that do not match. A fixed reconciliation layout makes mismatches visible each day, while deciding which group earns the credit and booking corrections stays with people.

synthesis.description: Confirmations of gas purchases and sales pass between marketing staff, counterparties and the groups that record the deals. A round starts when someone sends a copy of a confirmation or a transaction confirmation sheet for a sale, such as operational gas sold to a customer, or when a counterparty asks for confirmations it never received. The confirmation carries the volume, delivery point and period, and the recording group needs those details to book the deal; at times the sender is unsure how the information reaches that group.
steps: A gas sale or purchase is agreed with a counterparty.
The seller prepares or requests the confirmation sheet with volume, delivery point and period.
The confirmation is sent to the counterparty and a copy goes to the groups that record the deal.
The recording group books the deal from the copy.
A counterparty missing confirmations asks for them and the missing months are sent.

stalls.summary: A counterparty never received confirmations for several months of sales and had to raise it before they were sent.
The person sending details of a new operational gas sale was not sure how the information gets to the group that records it.

automation.approach: Generate the confirmation from the deal record when a sale or purchase is entered, send it to the counterparty, copy the recording groups from a standing distribution list, and keep a log of confirmations sent so a missing one shows up before the counterparty asks.
automation.rationale: The mail shows confirmations missed for whole months and a sender unsure where the details go. A standard confirmation message with the deal terms laid out and the recording groups already addressed fixes both for the people doing it now; automatic generation from the deal record follows once the system supports it. Checking terms and handling disputes stay with people.

synthesis.description: Employees ask their manager for days off or to be put down on the vacation calendar for particular dates. The manager replies granting the request, including short-notice days off, and reminds the person that a longer vacation should be planned in advance the same way as for everyone else in the group. Approved dates are recorded on the group's vacation calendar.
steps: An employee asks the manager for specific days off or to be added to the vacation calendar.
The manager checks the request against the group's coverage and other planned absences.
The manager replies approving the days, or sets the expectation that longer vacations are planned in advance.
The approved dates are entered on the vacation calendar.

automation.approach: A shared vacation calendar with a short request form that shows who else in the group is out on the requested dates, so the manager approves from one view and the approved dates are recorded on the calendar as part of the approval.
automation.rationale: The quotes show brief requests, approvals and entries on the vacation calendar; the work is checking coverage and recording dates, which a shared calendar layout supports. Approval stays a manager's call, as the guidance on planning longer vacations ahead shows.
